en: Second Act. Yajamāna = one who has performed a sacrifice; Kauśika.
"Prāyaprabhātā" means abounding in the characteristics of dawn; according to Amarasimha, "prāyaḥ" is used in the senses of abundance and conclusion (or end).
That very [word].
He establishes this sequentially with the verse beginning "by the darknesses" (*tamobhiḥ*), and so forth.
"When its life has passed" (*gatavayasi*) means when its setting is imminent. "About to blaze" (*jvaliṣyat*) refers to the period prior to the rising of smoke from that which is about to blaze.
"Are drunk" (*pīyante*) means they are covered.
The meaning is that the distinction between the directions is not known due to darkness.
It is an empirical fact that for a moment one enters into darkness between the setting of the moon and the dawn of the sun.

The magnet stone (*ayaskāntamaṇi*) is the attractor here, in whose proximity even iron, kusha grass, and so forth, though buried, rises up. *Karṣan* means "for the sake of attracting" (*karṣaṇāya*); [this is according to] Pāṇini 3.2.126: *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ*.
In the phrase "of the action" (*kriyāyāḥ*), the suffix *śatṛ* is used;
the meaning is that it does not produce the heat caused by drawing [the bowstring]. //1//
"Born," and so forth. *Palāṇḍu* is white garlic.

*Kiñcana* is a single indeclinable used in the sense of "also. *Aṅkurayanti* means they cause [it] to sprout, that is to say, they make it known. *Jīvātavaḥ* means those which have become life-restoring medicines. *Itaḥ* means in the west.
A spider (*lūtā*) is a weaver (*tantuvāya*); its similarity to a web (*tantuvitāna*) is due to the cause of the morning time, because its rays have departed.
A man whose clothes and other possessions have been stolen by a thief hides during the day on a mountain or similar place out of shame.
Thus is its meditative absorption (samādhi). //2//

"Digityādi" and so forth. "Even though unrisen" (*garbhite'pi*) means even when not yet appeared. "Those who inquire after a pleasant sleep" (*saukha-prasuptikāḥ*) refers to those who ask about a comfortable slumber;
the suffix *ṭhak* is applied here according to the rule *pṛcchatau susnātādibhyaḥ* (Pāṇini 4.4.1).
Through the pretext of the humming of bees within the lotus buds, there is the "sarasitya" (graceful charm) of the lakes, because they act as mutual flatterers. //3//
"Prācī," and so forth.
"Vibhramakarṇikāḥ" means those that serve as ear-ornaments for the purpose of playful charm (*vilāsa*);
the suffix *kan* is applied according to the rule "after *karṇa* and *lalāṭa*, [the suffix] *kan* is used when referring to an ornament. (Pāṇini 5.2.114).
They were like the fresh petals of such lotuses; according to Amarasimha, "saṃvartikā" means "a new petal. Regarding the phrase "two or three":
even though they arise one by one, this is a designation referring to each subsequent one together with all those that preceded it.

They reach [the state of] *uccarante* (emerging); the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to the rule "udaścaraḥ [sakarmakāt]" (Pāṇini 1.3.53). *Ucchvāsaḥ* means expansion. *Utsukatvam* refers to the desire for departure;
*autsukyam* is the inability to endure time [due to longing]. This is because they emerge together.
The sense is that they bloom even out of season by the power [of the fragrance] alone. //4//
"One, two," and so forth. "Astaṃ yatām" means "of those that have gone out of sight";
[the *Kāśikā* states: "'Astaṃ' is an indeclinable ending in the letter *m*, used in the sense of non-perception. (8)
The compound [is formed] by [the words] beginning with *kugati* (Pāṇini 2.2.18). *Eṣām* means "of these" [fingers]. *Gaṇanām* means "counting," in the sequence of one, two, three, and four.
*Kurvāṇeva* means "as if performing"; the suffix *śānac* is used here in the sense of cause (*hetau*). *Sāyam*.
In the first counting of her hands, she had contracted them like fingers with their thousand petals; in the second counting of those very same hands at dawn,
due to the absence of petals, they were like fingers once again.

The meaning is that he performed the spreading of the petals. As for "hundreds" (*śatāni*) and "thousand" (*sahasram*), because these possess fixed genders, they do not take the gender of the substantive; for example, "the Vedas are the authority" (*vedāḥ pramāṇam*).
As in the phrase "itivat": one, two, three, and four; of these, in sequence—that is, in regular order;
this is an illustration [extending] up to a thousand, [referring to] those things to be numbered.
Whether it concerns successive actions,
or merely the connection with the activity of arising and passing away,
or the connection with the property of having the form of succession;

Since simultaneity exists in the form of being mounted upon a single cognition, the formation of a *dvandva* compound by way of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) is established by that alone—just as in the expression, "Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa arrived in succession.

Furthermore, this very state of being mounted upon a single cognition is precisely what constitutes the simultaneity of the objects that serves as the cause for the *dvandva* compound; as it has been said:

Hari states: "When a single unified cognition of distinct entities arises as if they were interwoven, that is said to be the intention to express them together [in the forms of] dvandva and ekaśeṣa. Nor is the restriction to simultaneity limited solely to the connection with an action.
For we observe the use of the copulative compound even when there is a connection based on a mere attribute, as in the expression "the meritorious Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa. //5//
"Pratyāsanna," and so forth. *Sindhura* means an elephant; as stated in the *Amaraśeṣa*: "The two born from the ocean, the Viṣāṇin and the Kumbhira, are *sindhuras*. (13)
"Dense and crimson with vermilion"—
this is the speech [of the speaker] pointing toward the eastern quarter with her finger, saying, "The sky from here."

"Prācīnam" means relating to the eastern region; the sense is that it makes known "this is the east. [The suffix] *kha* is applied according to the rule "vibhāṣāñceradikstriyām" (Pāṇini 5.4.8). "Tat" means therefore. "Yāvad abhyudayate" means "I suspect it will rise"; [the form is used for the future].
"According to the rule *yāvatpurānipātayor laṭ* (Pāṇini 3.3.4), [the form] *kṛntati* refers to the *tarku*—that is, Viśvakarman;
this is due to the transposition of the initial and final syllables.
Now, as for the transposition of the initial and final [syllables]..."
"The word *bhavati* means a small rope, sand, or a plane," says the author of the *Nirukta*.
A *ṭaṅka* is an iron instrument for splitting stone; [it is] a chisel.
According to Amara, *pāṣāṇadāraka* means a stone-cutter;
by that [instrument], *unmṛjā* is carving (*takṣaṇa*);
by that, *rajyat* means becoming red; [this occurs] through rubbing.
Just as the body becomes red in an instant, so too the reflection (bimba) becomes [red] at that very moment; that is to say, it is produced by the cutting of the *rajas* [fiber]. The reflection—
"It rises as if being turned by Viśvakarman"—this is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). (18)//6//
"Even now" means even at this moment. The logical connection (*anvaya*) is: because there is no delay of time, therefore I am going.
"Sambhrāntaḥ" means agitated. "Ārya," etc. [follows].
Chāyā: Noble Śunaḥśepa, something both wonderful and terrifying is occurring. [Wonder and fear.]
Because of the two [factors] of being human and running away;
for although the animal's male organ is consecrated, it is nonetheless subject to the status of a Brāhmaṇa.
Regarding Śunaḥśepa,
because he was not yet favored by ascetic power (*tapas*), the ordinary [language] alone should be applied; [he was] refined by the grammatical systems of Kumāra, Pāṇini, and others.
It is considered refined for Brahmins,
Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, ministers, chamberlains, ascetics, actors,
and others who are not of low status.

Having stated, "It is employed," [it is so] because it has been said: "That which belongs to those who are low by action or by birth is called *prākṛta*. Furthermore, what is called *camatkāra* (aesthetic thrill) is the trembling of the body caused by fear and other such emotions; and he will state later: "*Camatkāra* is hidden..."
"The word *karaja* expresses their [the nails'] state.
(21) Thus, *camat* is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the sound of movement; according to the rule "an imitation is not followed by the particle *iti*" (22).
The term *gatisaṃjñā* refers to the compound [rule] "gatikāraka" (Pāṇini 1.4.60). *Chāyā*: Having heard that a certain Kṣatriya prince named Rāma had arrived today, she ran out out of curiosity.
A stone statue situated at the edge of the ascetic grove, having truly become human, has come right before me; upon seeing her,
I have even cast off my upper garment and bark cloth.
"I have fled. [He says this] laughing; the laughter arises because he is afraid even though there is no cause for fear. For this very reason, he says, "By good fortune indeed..."
A jestful remark.
Chāyā: May the noble one protect me from the mouth of this wicked Rākṣasī!

"May she protect"—that is, ward off; [here] the status of *apādāna* (ablative/source) applies according to the rule "for those [verbs] having the sense of warding off (*vāraṇa*), that which is desired (*īpsita*) [is the *apādāna*]. In this context, the term "Rākṣasī" refers to what is called "delusion" (*bhrānti*), due to delusion.

This is a sub-division (*sandhyantara*) of the *aṅga*; as it has been said: "Error (*bhrānti*) is a cognition of reversal (*viparyayajñāna*), because there is no certainty regarding the consequence (*prasaṅga*). (25) Thus, by the word "trembling" (*vepamāna*), this fear (*bhaya*), known as a sub-division of the *sandhyantara*, is indicated.
As it has been said: "Fear, however, is sudden terror" (26).
[The word] "wives" (dārān) [is used].
The plural number is used either because of the multiplicity residing in the parts,
or even in the case of a single [entity].

"Because of the statement of the learned: 'The great esteem shown toward a single individual, as if toward many, is produced by specific qualities, or by the attribution of multiplicity [to that one individual]';"—[Chāyā:
"I hear [the words] of Śatānanda, the family priest of Janaka's lineage."
Mother; then, then; *cāritra* = chastity (specifically wifely devotion); *dīrghatapas* = Gautama;
of the sense-organ = of the mind.
Weakness is instability; likewise, that which exists in the form of a stone statue is "untransformed," while that which is undergoing transformation is "ripened."
Sin is characterized as darkness because it is destroyed by light; liberation is emancipation. On this point, the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa states: "Because of her infidelity, she was cursed by Indra."
"O King of kings, formerly turned to stone by her husband, Ahalyā was released from the curse upon seeing Rāma.
(28) [In this verse, the suffix] *ṇic* is used in the sense of "uncovering" (*unmīlya*), followed by the suffix *lyap*; [this occurs] because of the departure of fear.
Chāyā: Oh, by the grace of my noble lord, I am established once more in the world of the living! Nevertheless, the fever of apprehension still does not leave me; therefore, please rest for a moment.
"Friend," and so forth. [This refers to] the Brāhmaṇa who has studied the Vedas.

"Fear is of no consequence" means that for a Brahmin who is by nature timid, fear arises even without a cause; "therefore" (tat) means because there is an absence of a cause for fear; "himself" (ātmānam) refers to the mind.
"Settle it" means make it healthy.
"Rest for a long time" refers to the limb named *prāpti* (attainment), because its nature consists in the arrival at well-being.
As it has been said: "Attainment is the arrival of happiness" (30).
[Objection: How is it that even the Blessed Lord Hari exhibits the nature of a deer amidst the shimmering mirage of sense-objects?
It is being mimicked!
The word *jhalañjhalī* refers to the current by way of imitating the sound of the flow of water.
"Deception" (*viḍambanam*) means the delusion that something is a means to happiness even when it is not; the sense is that even Indra fell into such error.
Regarding Indra as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), he says "insignificant" (*alpīyān*) and so forth. "World" (*loka*) means people; as Amarasimha states:
"The word *loka* refers to the world and to people. (Amarakośa 3.1).
The singular number is used for the genus (jātāvekavacanam).
He himself explains its smallness by means of a question, beginning with "How," and so forth.

How so? If it is asked "how so?", the meaning is as follows. He provides the answer with the words beginning "aihika" and so forth. That which occurs here [in this world] is *aihika*; the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied according to the rule for the group beginning with *adhyātma*, because that very group contains the word [in question], and for that very reason...
Arising from conditions;
by means of "ascertainment and relish"— that is, by means of the experience of the certainty of permanence—
those who are "greedy," meaning the deluded.
The verbal root is *lubha* in the sense of "deluding" (34). The word *rātri* is indicative of time; the meaning is that a great amount of time is being rendered fruitless.
The substitution of *ṇa* for *na* occurs according to the rule *hanteratpūrvasya* (35).
Although such a smallness [of the offense] remains established, he first intends to demonstrate how Indra’s lack of discipline is greater than that of the world.
He demonstrates the cause of the world's lack of discipline with the words "but" (kintu): by means of things that are "artificial" (āhāryaiḥ), meaning unreal,
and comparable to borrowed items.
Or, for Indra who is being summoned—that is, being brought face to face—he demonstrates the causes of his lack of discipline with the words "What more...
The meaning is that prosperity and authority are the causes of pride. To the question, "What fault is there in merely seeing him? [the answer follows].

He says: "Visual delight," and so forth. "Visual delight" (*cakṣuḥprīti*) means the delight born of seeing. The second case ending is used because *anu* functions as a *karmapravacanīya* (prepositional particle) in the sense of a characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
The meaning is: "at that very moment when visual pleasure arises.
The others—the nine states beginning with mental attachment—are as follows.
As it has been said: "First is the pleasure of the eye, then the attachment of the mind, then the mental resolve;
followed by loss of sleep, emaciation, withdrawal from sense objects, and the destruction of shame;
then madness, fainting, and death—these are the ten stages of love."
Thus [he said].
Chāyā: I believe that this is the ripening of the merit of this hermit’s wife during the absence of the noble Rāma.
The reason.
Chāyā: Noble sir, I am eager to hear even the second part of this speech of yours.
"‘There is [a city] in Kiṣkindhā,’ and so forth; beginning from here until ‘I heard this from the mouth of my father Viśvāmitra’ (38).”
The limb named *udbheda* consists in the disclosure of what was hidden; as it has been said: "Udbheda is the disclosure of what was hidden.
*Acchabhallāḥ* means bears.
Golāṅgūlas are a specific type of monkey with long tails and black faces.
Commentary— here and there.
"Especially," and so forth. *Avaskanda* means contempt or an attack during a vulnerability; regarding this, the *Nītivākyāmṛta* states: "In times of calamity..."

"Or, when one is negligent, there may be an enemy's invasion or a sudden assault. (40) Thus, [the meaning is: a deceitful person is unworthy of affection, how much more so one who is an enemy of his father?
The sense is that the enmity toward one's father must be avenged by all means.
He dispels the doubt regarding invincibility with the words beginning "tvadīya" (your own) and so forth.
*Pauruṣam* refers to the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*); for a sentiment flows away when it is squeezed.
For us, there is neither the attainment of the desired nor the avoidance of the undesired.
Thus he says: "Nor even," and so forth.
A *sāmanta* is a neighboring enemy. *Laghvī* means swift; that which has a *samutthā*, or arrival, characterized by speed, is [so described].
When you desire to advance against the enemy, [the ocean], due to its intervening presence,
is neither a helper nor an obstacle.
The meaning is "quick arrival.

*Virāddhamaṇḍalena* means "by one who has offended the circle [of states]"—that is, by one who harms everyone. *Anarthānubandhi* means "consequent upon misfortune"; [it refers to] "one who hates the circle [of states]."
"One who is affectionate may perish even if he has committed no offense," says Kauṭilya; and Kāmandaka likewise: "Greedy, cruel, lazy, untruthful, negligent, timid, unstable, and foolish—"
And one who treats warriors with contempt is considered an enemy easily destroyed by [the mere prospect of] happiness. (42)
Thus [it is said]. He says, "Not only is he [unhelpful],
but his followers as well are indeed unhelpful," by means of the passage beginning with "Furthermore" (kiñca) and so forth.
"The bull, the chariot, the ornament," and so forth; here, by means of two halves [of verses], respectively,
[the qualities] of the Lord [are described].

He speaks of poverty and the causes for receiving assistance: "Like a chariot, [he is] a chariot," because he is a means of transport; "residing in the same abode" refers to Śiva as well, because he dwells in the city of Alakā. As it has been said: "Your dwelling place to be visited is named Alakā, belonging to the lords of the Yakṣas."
"With its palaces washed by the moonlight from the head of Hara situated in the outer garden"— thus [it is described]. He himself is wealthy,
and his friend Kubera is also present nearby.
The causes for the states of being a benefactor and being benefited. //7//
Chāyā: Oh, how skillful is the elder bear in his employment of counsel and his cleverness in jesting! What happened next?
[In private]—secretly.
"By his permission" means by Jāmbavān’s permission; according to Amarasimha, "rahas" and "upāṃśu" both mean "in secret.
[He was] with difficulty.
"Durgam" means that which is difficult to traverse, as it is derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍa* according to the rule "suduroradhikaraṇe" (Pāṇini 3.2.48).

It is said that in former times, even the sages dwelling on Mount Ṛṣyamūka— though their staffs, water-pots, robes, and other belongings had been seized by the youthful Vālin— were treated otherwise [with hostility] toward him.
Being unable to curse him, they cursed him, saying, "May your head split asunder upon climbing this."
The story of the Rāmāyaṇa should be investigated. (46) Shadow: Noble sir, he who is heard of as the son of the Wind-god and the wrestler of the three worlds—
The grammatical connection is: "He who is heard [of] is Mārutin. The word *malla* signifies "excellent" (47). [This is] a question by way of intonation.
Chāyā: Noble sir, let it be as it may.
The master is indeed a master. Having abandoned him, it would not be fitting to accept one so contrary to such a highly fortunate man.
Even if the master were wicked, he is still the master.
The meaning is that it must indeed be abandoned.
Regarding "having laughed," and so forth: Hanumān’s action is prompted solely by what ought to be done, and not otherwise.
The remark "in the form of betraying one's master" is said in jest. From this point until the end of the passage beginning with "jaṃ guruputto vā" (48),
the purpose is to avoid the charge that Sugrīva’s acceptance [of Hanumān] was improper.

The limb named *yukti* (reasoning) arises from the determination of the meaning in the form of propriety through the statement regarding the pursuit of the Guru’s son. As it has been said: "Reasoning (*yukti*) is the thorough deliberation of meanings" (49). *Āñjaneya* is the offspring of *Añjanā*; [the suffix] *ṅyaṅ* is applied after feminine bases...
*Ḍhak*: (50) *adhīyan* means studying or practicing without difficulty; the suffix *śatṛ* is applied according to the rule *iṅdhāryoḥ śatrakṛcchriṇi*.
*Sāhāyakam* means assistance; the suffix *vuñ* is applied according to the statement *sahāyād veti vaktavyam*.
Regarding the term "one who knows the intention":
because following the son of another's wife is unworthy of being expressed by the literal function of words (*vācyavṛtti*), it is [only] intended (*abhipreta*).
Chāyā: Hum, it is indeed appropriate that the teacher’s son or a fellow student should be followed.
What then? What then?

*Upajāpa* means *bheda* (sowing dissension); according to Amarasimha, "Furthermore, *bheda* and *upajāpa* are synonyms" (53). By that [dissension], *jarjara* means weakened or loosened. *Pratigraha* refers to the rear force; according to Amarasimha, "*pratigraha* is the rear of the army" (54).
Thus says Amara.
Chāyā: "How is it that even that Rākṣasa has not abandoned the duty of a friend?
How so? The construction is "even though he is a Rākṣasa"; this "how" expresses wonder.

"What is being said?"—the remainder is that his greatness is impossible to describe. "Rāvaṇa indeed"—by this word, which emphasizes his renown, [it is implied]: "If even one who is free from worldly attributes can please the world, how much more so [one who possesses them]?"
The greatness of that [state] has been described as "in the presence of affection" (*snehopādhau*).
He states that very thing in the verse beginning with *priyākartum* and so forth, according to the rule:
"After *sukha*, *priya*, and others, when expressing compliance" (*ānulomye*).
The sense is that one should perform [the practice] out of compliance (*ānulomya*), and not with a desire for results.
By the expression "to anyone whatsoever" (*kasmaicana*), it is indicated that this applies even toward a deity, as a statement of disregard.
He speaks of Rāvaṇa’s lack of meanness: by the rule "rucyarthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 1.4.33), he is designated as the recipient (*sampradāna*);
he who satisfies the world even by the severing of his own head is Rāvaṇa alone in this world, and no other.
This is the meaning: he whose heads are tender and new because they have been repeatedly cut off;
who is *vilakṣa*—meaning ashamed—and whose activity consists of bowing down and so forth.
Such a thing:
some indescribable deformity, because it is not tender due to being produced without interruption;
[this refers to] those who have been born again.

Even though [the elements] that have been elided are different [from those remaining], the statement of non-difference is due either to their belonging to the same class (sājātya) or to the status of being like the original (sthānivadbhāva). //8//
Chāyā: And then?
Suketu: There was a yakṣa named Suketu.
Chāyā: That a woman possesses the strength of a thousand nāgas—this has never been heard before.
And so it continued.
The Kulapati—the one who initiates the lineage (kula) in the form of the transmission of knowledge—[says]: "I know him as Rāmabhadra. Chāyā: [I] know [him as] Rāmabhadra.
He has indeed descended upon the Rākṣasas;
the meaning is that he has appeared for the purpose of slaying the demons.
"One whose mantras are perfected" means one for whom meditation alone yields the fruit; as it has been said:
In the *Brahmānandanāthīya*, mantras are said to be of five kinds: *siddha*, *susiddha*, *ārṣa*, *pauruṣa*, and *śābara*; among these, the first is...
"It bestows the fruit of mere meditation" (57).
The meaning is that it bestows the fruit independently of the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) and its ritual application.

Of Brahman-jyotis— that is, of Brahman whose nature is light— such [an appearance] is a transformation (vivarta) consisting of sound, which is of the nature of a false modification; however, in reality:
The meaning is "light alone"; as it has been said: "The Veda is Śiva, Śiva is the Veda.
There is wonder because of the demonstration of piercing many targets with a single arrow.
By the word *pārāyaṇa*, he expresses study in its entirety.
"Regarding the words *sākalya* and *asaṅga*, [Amara] states: 'The terms *pārāyaṇa* and *parāyaṇa* [denote completion].
(59)" Chāyā: "I believe that Rāma possesses both the powers *Balā* and *Atibalā* along with the weapon-deities consisting of mantras."
"It shall pass on.
These are two specific mantras named Balā and Atibalā.
They are the destroyers of hunger and other such afflictions; as it is said in the Rāmāyaṇa: "O Rāma, hunger and thirst shall never befall you while you recite Balā and Atibalā on the road."
"O Raghava! (60) Thus [he says]. Chāyā: Noble sir, am I not saying that if it were by his own power alone...
Since the sciences of weaponry are indeed his own, why then [should he seek help] from Rāghava for the pacification of his obstacles?
Does the venerable Kauśika offer this as a mark of respect? Or rather, is this merely the killing of a snake by means of a guest?
This is respect.

It was employed for the purpose of warding off obstacles to the sacrifice. *Prāhuṇika* means a guest; as Amarasimha states: "An *āveśika*, a *prāhuṇika*, or a *atithi* is one who has come to the house. (61) This amounts to saying it was like the killing of a serpent. When a serpent is killed by a guest, the householder attains well-being.
The sense is that, were the opposite the case, the guest alone would die; likewise, in the opposing scenario, Rāma himself would die.
"By one's own application" means by an application performed by oneself (*svakartṛka-prayoga*). "By pupils" means having pupils as the agents (*antevāsikaraṇaka*);
when it is said "having pupils as the agents," the genitive case in "of the pupils" (*antevāsinām*) is applied according to Pāṇini 2.3.65: *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*.
It may be so; "prayoga" means "purpose," with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) implied.

Alternatively, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*): the application (*prayoga*) has the student as its agent, with "of knowledge" (*vidyāyāḥ*) being the ellipsis; this is according to the rule "when both [agent and object] are applicable, [the sixth case is used] for the object" (*ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*).
The genitive case is not used by rule; however, because knowledge (*vidyā*) functions as the object (*karman*), the genitive occurs there.
That very [point].
He demonstrates this with the words beginning "in the places" (*sthāneṣu*).
"In the places" means in suitable locations; "having taken" means having received from the ocean.
Water cast by the clouds becomes the pearl-gem within oyster shells, but not that which is cast by its own waves.

Up to the point where "ādāyaśuktiṣu" is a single compound word: either it means those whose *dāya* (giving) is *ā-*, i.e., complete purity (*nairmalya*), and they are also *śuktayaḥ* (oyster shells); or [it refers to the root] *daip*.
