And the Grāvastotra chant is "bhaṅgurāvataḥ" (140). //28//
The absence of hearing [the Veda] is due to his attachment to gazing upon the forest.
With reference to those in the forest-dwelling stage (vānaprastha), he says "three times," and so forth.
"Three times" means at the times of morning, midday, and the evening twilight; the accusative case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.5 (kālādhvanoḥ).
"Vāraḥ means repetition of an action," according to Vardhamāna; by this, the time suitable for that [action] is indicated. *Abhiṣuṇvate* = they bathe.
*Sthitīḥ* = means of livelihood. *Vanyaiḥ* = those things wholesome in the forest (*vane sādhubhiḥ*). "In that... [the suffix *yat* is used].

The suffix *yat* [is applied] in the sense of "good" (*sādhu*). The meaning is that they subsist solely on bulbs, roots, and so forth. *Aiṇeyyām* means "belonging to the female deer (*eṇī*). [From] *eṇyā*...
The suffix *ḍhañ* [is applied here]. They settle down, that is, they sit down; sleeping, however, occurs even on the bare ground. "Tāravīm" means belonging to a tree;
they clothe themselves, that is, they cover themselves. Thus it has been said:
In the *Nibandhanasarvasva*: "The forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) who observes celibacy (*brahmacārī*), bathing at the three periods of the day (*triṣavaṇa*),

clothed in rags or skins, subsisting on uncultivated field-grown grains such as *nīvāra* and *śyāmāka*, [performs] the rites to be accomplished through fire-offerings, the giving of alms, and the honoring of gods, guests, ancestors, dependents, and those who have arrived at his hermitage."
He should offer libations; he himself should eat food prepared without salt;

he should sleep on the ground alone. (146) By stating, "The duties mentioned in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*) also apply here, provided they do not conflict," [it is established that] the skin of the black antelope (*aiṇeyī*)...
The skin has been described;
regarding this, Āpastamba states: "For a Brāhmaṇa, it should be the skin of a black antelope or a spotted deer. (148)

"In the realm of the skin" (*cārmaṇe*) means "consisting of skin," that is to say, in that which does not effect the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkārākaraṇe*). "Blessed" (*dhanyā*) means "meritorious.
"Free from passion and darkness" (*vītarajastamāḥ*) means "one from whom passion has utterly departed"; [this suffix] is used in the sense of excellence (*atiśāyane*).

*Tamap*: (149) Or, it means that from her *rajas* and *tamas* have departed; the sense is that she is purely *sāttvika*. *Āhlādate* = *āhlādayati*; the causative sense is internalized [within the verb]. //29//
"Once again that very same thing," refers to the passage beginning with, "O Rāmabhadra, how long must we wait while looking on? (150).
"Katham" and so forth: the word "katham" expresses wonder at the fact that time is not perceived due to the curiosity of gazing upon the forest. "Āhnika" means pertaining to the day.
"Pratyanantara" means immediate or proximate.
"Uddāma," and so forth. By "vyatikara" (intermingling), [the meaning is] "yoga" (union); "prakrīḍantaḥ" means "blazing.
Due to the influence of the prefix (*upa-*), it carries the sense of "blazing," since verbal roots have multiple meanings. "Jaṭālā" means as if possessing censurable matted hair.

Because they lack the refinement of oil and the like, they are dry and thus reddish-brown and entangled with one another; for this very reason, these hairs, which are censurable, are here referred to by the word *jaṭā*.
The meaning is that just as those [hairs] are difficult to look upon, so too are the flames.
In the rule "jaṭāghaṭākālāḥ kṣepe" (Pāṇini 5.2.109), the suffix *lac* is applied because [the word *jaṭā*] belongs to the *sidhma*-class.
*Jāṅgalataṭī* is ground characterized by qualities such as being waterless; as it has been said: "That which has very little water and grass..."
"A region with much wind and abundant sunshine is to be known as a *jāṅgala* [arid] land"— (154); in such a place,
they are "silent" (*niṣkūjāḥ*), meaning devoid of sound, due to the excess of heat.
Those [regions] in which there are *koyaṣṭis*—a particular species of bird.

It is a well-known tenet of the scriptures that a mirage arises from the conjunction of terrestrial heat and the rays of the sun. For this very reason, they are of a cruel nature, meaning they are difficult to behold; for this very reason, they are empty.
This is due to the non-appearance of objects or the absence of the movement of living beings.
*Āyus* is the capacity for perceiving forms; *karman*, which is merit (*puṇya*), is that which causes it. The meaning is that they destroy it, because when the cause is destroyed...
Because of the destruction of the effect; the meaning is that objects are not manifested by mirages. This is to be connected with the phrase "amūrdhig" (not above). //30//
*Pratyavekṣaṇam* means *pratipālanam* (guarding).
"In the middle" (*madhye*) and so forth: "in the middle of the sky" (*madhyevyoma*) means "in the midst of the sky";
this is an *avyayībhāva* compound according to the rule *pāre madhye ṣaṣṭhyā vā*. The sequence is connected with both hanging down and pulling up. *Svairaṃ svairam* means slowly.
"Slowly"; according to Amara, "svaira" means both "slow" and "independent.
At the setting of the sun, the forward movement of the shadow is thus imagined. Furthermore, *chāyā* is also the name of the Sun's beloved wife. [This refers to] one whose destruction is imminent.
"The possession is stolen by another"—this is the worldly consensus. //31//
"O child," and so forth. The word *madhyandina* denotes midday;
the meaning is that the duration of time is known to be prior to midday, not after it.
The word *madhyandina* is grammatically correct here because it is included in the list beginning with *utsa*.
He says that very thing with the verse beginning "gagana" and so forth. "Śikhām" means the summit. "From the Udayādri" (the Mountain of Sunrise).
"Kaṣṭam" means with difficulty. It is well known that ascending is difficult while descending is easy. //32//
"Parāpatanam" means "the arrival.
"If it were so" means "if the Rākṣasas were to assemble.
"Kalpānta," etc., refers to the slayer—meaning the one who strikes down—those who cause obstacles to the sacrifice.
The genitive case is used for the object according to the rule *jāsiniprahaṇa* (Pāṇini 2.3.56).
Although the Rākṣasas are present, the word "of these" (*amīṣām*) is used because they are the subject under discussion. [He protected] even the earth; indeed, he protected only the hermitage.

The word "na" (not) has the sense of the particle "api" (even). Of this rite for pacification (*śāntikarman*), the preliminary limb (*pūrvāṅga*) is the day of merit (*puṇyāha*); that itself is the auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
"[Ādadhātu]" means "may it nourish" or "may it sustain."

The meaning is that at the beginning of this rite, which consists of the slaying of all *rākṣasas*, this minor slaying is for the purpose of pronouncing the "auspicious day" (*puṇyāhavācana*). On this point, the *Kūrmapurāṇa* states:
"One should perform all rites preceded by the pronouncement of 'well-being' (*svastivācana*). (159)
Thus [ends the thirty-third].
Unable to tolerate the phrase "if it were so" (160) and others, which suggests that the arrival of the Rākṣasa is merely a possibility, he says: "Laughing," and so forth.
"Visaṃsthula" means agitated. By the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even Kauśika," the omniscience of the Sage is indicated.
He treats one who lacks foresight as worthy of respect and considers him to be ignorant of the future;
the underlying thought is that "truly, Rākṣasas will assemble."
He states omniscience itself with the words "ignorance" and so forth:
"of ignorance" means of the *tūla* (cotton-like) ignorances; "of the seed" means of the root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*).
The seer’s eye is supersensuous knowledge; he caused it to enter— that is, he made it penetrate—
even that which is past and future.
The meaning is that one knows [the object] as if it were present. //34//
"Known," and so forth. "Known" (*prajñāta*) means directly realized (*sākṣātkṛta*).

"Conducive to heaven" (*svargīya*) means beneficial for heaven (*svargāya hitaiḥ*); [the suffix] *cha* is applied according to Pāṇini 5.1.1. [This refers to] one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
He dispels the doubt that there is no qualification for ritual action by saying "by the [initiation] rule" (samaya);
this also lasts until the cessation of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Because the conduct prescribed for one's own stage of life (*āśrama*) must be performed;

regarding this, the *Yogavāsiṣṭha* states: "Whether one is a knower or ignorant, as long as the body is sustained, so long must that which is prescribed for one's caste and stage of life be carried out."
"Karma for the sake of liberation. (162) By the word "plays," the absence of desire for fruits is expressed. //35//
He states that very point with the words "moistened" and so forth.
"Kuṇḍalita" means marked with a line [indicating] that it is to be rejected.
Triśaṅku was a king of the Ikṣvāku lineage who, desiring heaven, [ascended] with his physical body.

Having been rejected by his own guru Vasiṣṭha, he approached Viśvāmitra; having performed sacrifices for him, he was sent by him toward heaven, where he was repulsed by Indra as a traitor to his guru.
He fell to the ground; then, having begun to create another heaven out of that anger, the sage desisted at Indra's request and [created] a world for Triśaṅku.
"He fashioned [it]"—thus the narrative is to be connected. From the word *triśaṅku*, the suffix *aṇ* is applied in the four senses according to the rule *kopadhācca*.
For one who possesses the power to create worlds such as heaven, there is no dependence upon heaven.
This is the state of being. Even though the Sage is not present, the designation "this one" is used for the purpose of indicating his entrance. //36//

"By their own," and so forth. "By their own" (*svābhiḥ*) means by those belonging to themselves. "Making [them] successful in their purpose" (*kṛtārthayan*) means removing invalidity characterized by non-performance; this is the reason for performance. //37//
"Clad in the attire of one initiated" means wearing the black antelope skin and so forth.
"Of the ritual," etc.: "of that which is heard" refers to the Śrauta [ritual].
"By signs" means by marks, such as the antelope skin and so forth. //38//
"Completed," and so forth. "For now" means the intention is that we shall explain the future goal later.
"Much" is an adverbial modifier of the action. "This" refers to [the work] by me.
Being made [an heir]; "dāyāda" means son, as in "mārīca";
according to Amarasimha, "dāyāda" refers to both a son and a kinsman (Amara-kośa 1.5.4).
Because he had fled, he was as good as dead.
The state of being killed (*hatatva*);

[the form] *ghāniṣyate* is derived from the root *han* with the causative suffix *ṇic*, in the passive voice, with the future suffix *lṛṭ*; [this is formed] by the rule beginning with *syasicsīyuṭ* (Pāṇini 6.4.62).

The *ciṇvadiṭ* augment is applied, and by the rule "ho hanteḥ" (Pāṇini 7.3.54), there is *kutva* substitution. Because the *ciṇvadiṭ* augment is considered as if non-existent (*asiddhavat*) by the rule "asiddhavadatrābhāt" (Pāṇini 6.4.22), the *ṇi*-affix is elided by the rule "ṇeraniṭi" (Pāṇini 6.4.51).
Then, by the rule "ata upadhāyāḥ" (Pāṇini 7.2.116), there is *vṛddhi*. *Pāṇaukṛtya* means having taken [her] by the hand, i.e., having married her; [the word *nityam* follows].

In the phrase "haste pāṇāv upayamane," the suffix *lyap* is applied because [the word *hasta*] functions as a *gati*. It is both "one" (*ekam*) and "bride-price" (*śulkam*); the compound is formed according to the rule beginning with "pūrvakāla-" (Pāṇini 2.1.49).
Thus, *ekaśulkam* means that of which the sole price (*kevalamūlyam*) is the bride-price itself.
She was addressed in that manner; the meaning is that destruction itself is the toll (*śulka*), and nothing else.
According to Amara, "the word *eka* [is used in the senses of] primary, other, and exclusive. Regarding "in the directions of the gods' works":
the meaning is "in those directions in which the works of the gods exist."
"Vidhātāsmahe" means "we shall perform.
This is the limb known as *samādhāna* (resolution),
because by describing the excellence of Rāmabhadra’s heroism, it constitutes his *utsāha* (enthusiasm).

Because of the continuous connection of the seed; as it has been said: "The arrival of the seed is composure" (YS 1.32). Here, the arrival (*āgama*) of the seed means its continuous connection (*anusandhāna*). //39//

"eṣa" and so forth. "Vaihārika" means suitable for dwelling (*vihāra*); the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule "tadarhati" (Pāṇini 5.1.63). "Veṣa" means attire or appearance. "Āntaraṃ tattvaṃ" means the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
By means of observing this...
That is to say, joy arises as if through the experience of supreme bliss. //40//
"By you two," and so forth. "Abhinirvṛtti" means accomplished;
"yogakṣema" refers to that which possesses the acquisition of what has not been obtained and the preservation of what has been obtained. "Hetayaḥ" means weapons.
"Prakriyā" means manner or method.
The distinction is this: let them have as their sole fruit the mere indication of sovereignty, because even weapons must be provided by kings. //41//
"Kaccit," and so forth:
[the question is] whether these two, who have experienced every luxury in palaces of jewels,
find contentment in leaf-huts or in roots, tubers, and the like.
The meaning is "he knows.
Regarding the phrase "delightful," etc.: "to determine" means to ascertain.
"Transcending the two" means transcending rajas and tamas; the meaning is that it is purely sattvic.
"Furthermore, *sthāṇḍila* refers to those who are free from passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*), having transcended the two. (178)—thus says Amara. [This is stated] in the *Ānandalaharī*.
The meaning is that there was no discrimination between what is pleasant and what is unpleasant. //42//
"Ākūtam" means intention, which has the result of providing encouragement; and the encouragement is: "You two alone are the dwarfs."
Thus, by means of this indirect statement (*parokti*):

"here," and so forth. The Sage (*muni*)—namely Nārāyaṇa—having become Vāmana, performed austerities (*atapta*), meaning he accumulated ascetic merit (*tapa*). This is the *karmakartari* (passive-reflexive) construction. (179)

In the *Laghu-śabdendu-śekhara* (180), it is stated that because of the rule "tapas-tapaḥ-karma-kasya-eva" (Pāṇini 1.3.26), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) applies due to the treatment as a reflexive object (*karmavadbhāva*);
furthermore, by the rule "tapo-'nutāpe-ca" (Pāṇini 3.1.65), there is an absence of the *ciṇ* affix. [This applies] in the case of the agent who is also the object (*karmakartṛ*).
The essential meaning of the *Kāśikā* is that [the suffix -ti] denotes the act of producing (*tadarthajanana*).
(183) *Avalokya* means having perceived or known. Regarding *cirāt*: previously, the Blessed One...
Vāmana was the presiding witness;
from that time on, their eyes were opened by meditation.
Today, because he himself is present in your form, those who have accomplished what was to be achieved have their eyes opened.
The sense is that they "existed.
From this point onward, [the author says] "I cast [it] elsewhere" (184).
Thus ends the *aṅga* (dramatic element) named *bheda* (sowing dissension), which consists of the instigation of Rāmabhadra;
as it has been said: "Bheda is considered to be instigation. //43//
*Unmanībhavataḥ* means "becoming joyful"; the suffix *cvi* and the elision of the *s* are applied according to the rule *arurmanaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.4.51).
*Aye* is used at the beginning of the sentence.
*Prāgbhavīyam* means "relating to a previous birth"; the suffix *cha* is applied according to the rule *prākkrītācchaḥ* (Pāṇini 5.1.1). *Anyataḥ* means "incidentally."
There is a contrast with what has been previously mentioned, and the subsequent context is relevant because its purpose is to convey that "this is the time for the arrival of the night-stalkers.
As for the phrase beginning with "How so?": the mountain of sunrise itself is Kāśmīra—a particular region—and therein...

Of the twilight, which has the form of a field of saffron; its being "first" is the reason for the bouquet's worthiness of respect. That initiation rite in which the hand follows the hand is so described; from the hand...
The meaning is "by bringing it into the hand"; here, in the sūtra beginning with "dvitīyā" (Pāṇini 2.1.24),
because it is included by the word "ādi" (and so forth),
the compound is formed according to the rule "mayūravyaṃsakādayaśca" (Pāṇini 2.1.72).
The meaning is that sunset has drawn near.

He states this very point in the passage beginning with "this too" (*ayam api*). "Dyed with *kaṣāya*" means *kāṣāya*; the meaning is "dyed like lacquer" (*karṇavat rakta*); for *kaṣāya* [also] refers to a sweet [taste].

"Rakta" means "red," according to the *Vaijayantī* (189). "Visṛmarāḥ" means "pervading," from the rule "sṛghasyadaḥ kmarac" (190). And that [darkness] is indeed *timira* (darkness), because it is similar in nature to *ūrṇā*—the wool of sheep and the like; "ūrṇā... [is used here].
According to Amarasimha, "meṣādilomni" means wool; by that [term],
"[jarjharopāntam]" means having frayed edges, because there is a contradiction in their occupying the same location.
Pervasiveness is the cause of its being obstructive.
*Kalaviṅkyaḥ* means sparrows; *tāsām*, "of them"; *kākubhiḥ* means by notes born of joy;
for "a *kāku* is a modification [of voice] in a woman."
According to Amarasimha, "dhvani" [means] sound arising from grief, fear, and so forth (192); by means of those [sounds],
"nāndīkarāṇi" means those that produce auspicious musical instruments, for "nāndī" refers to an auspicious occasion.

According to the *Viśvaprakāśa*, [the word *vādya* means] "instruments"; by the rule *divāvibhā-* (Pāṇini 3.2.21), the suffix *ṭa* is applied to the root *kṛ* in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) after the word *nāndī*. Of kings...
The worldly convention is that *nāndīs* are performed at both the exit and the entrance;
"he gathers" means he draws [the audience] in. //44//
"Mantra," and so forth. "Consisting of the three Vedas" (*trayīmaya*) is the reason for his being the sanctifier (*saṃskartṛ*).
[The word] *tanvan* means "for the sake of extending" (*tananāya*); here the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is used in the sense of a causal factor (*hetau*). //45//
"By the heat," and so forth: "by the heat" means by solar [rays]; "scorched" means burnt;
"extinguished" means calmed; for that very reason, they are "dark-blue" (mecaka), i.e., blue.
"Manifests" means it brings about its manifestation; it is itself also blue.
The meaning is that it comes into being. //46//

"Kāñcid" and so forth. "Kāñcid" means indescribable. By means of the causes that are the flames of the sacrificial fires, masses of smoke pervade [the space], making the sides of the directions visible; this refers to the smoke.
The state of being a *valabhī* (roof-ridge) is due to its function as a coverer; Keśava states: "The word *bhitti* [is used] for a wall (*kuḍya*) and for a side.
(196) "The young students are heard"—this is by means of the recognition of their voices, thinking, "This is he, this is he."
The meaning is "they are known. By metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), the word *svādhyāya* refers to the act of recitation (*adhyayana*). *Dīrghān* means "long";
*pratimuhuḥ* means "repeatedly" (*muhurmuhuḥ*); *drāghayantaḥ* means "making long," that is, making [the sounds] protracted.

By the rule "priyasthira" (Pāṇini 6.4.157), there is the substitution of *drāgh* for the word *dīrgha*. Regarding this, the method of instruction states: "One should know that the third pressing (*savana*) is loud; and that [recitation] located at the head is always [loud]."
It is that which is to be employed. //47//
"Unmuktābhiḥ," and so forth. "Divasam" means throughout the entire day; the accusative case is used here to denote continuous duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*).
"Niculitam" means covered. The blazing of the ocean occurs due to the presence of the submarine fire (*aurva*) and its jewels. Its variegated nature arises from its possession of many colors. //48//
Disgust arises precisely from the degradation of that which was once excellent.

He states this very point in the passage beginning with "splendor" (*tejas*): that which consists of splendor becomes, at one time or another, composed of darkness (*tamas*); therefore, there is diversity.

*Kośa* means the body; as it is said: "The word *kośa*—which is not feminine—is used for a bud, a sword, a treatise, a mass of wealth, a house, the body, the private parts, the scrotum, the fetus, a book, and the sheath of a sword" (200).
Vaijayantī (200) // 49 //
"Cūḍā" and so forth. "Vivarāṇi" refers to the hollows of anthills.
"From the sun-stone" (*sūryakāntāt*) means having left the sun-stone; this is the ablative case used with the elision of a *lyap* suffix (denoting a prior action).
"Enters" (*niviśate*) means it goes inside; this is an expression [used] because of the heat of separation.

The term *nerviśaḥ* (202) is in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). *Śalkayantaḥ* means "breaking into pieces. The meaning is that the lamps shine like sparks from the fire of twilight produced by the friction of the powerful day and night on both sides.
The meditative absorption on that [object] arises from the emergence of sparks when rubbing stone and so forth. //50//

"Viśvam," and so forth. When there is darkness (*dhvānte*), that which is visual (*cākṣuṣam*)—meaning graspable by the eye—the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule "in the remaining cases" (*śeṣe*). "Set" (*astam*) means it is not seen. For (*hi*), because there is a unity with the darkness (*timiraikyam*). He explains this very point:

By the words "conditioned" (*aupādhikī*) and so forth: "conditioned" means that direction (*dik*), which is in reality one, appears as divided due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the sun; in the absence of those [adjuncts], it is the essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The sense is that they remain thus.

By "sharp" (paṭubhiḥ) is meant "skilled"; by "excellent senses" (akṣottaraiḥ) is meant those with praiseworthy faculties. Even so, causes of fear such as snakes and the like are perceived; the meaning is that suspicion of snakes and such arises in an inappropriate place. "Apaghana" means a limb or member.

The term *apaghana* is a nipāta (irregular formation) meaning "limb" (*aṅga*). The meaning is that a person is not known by the arrangement of their physical parts, but rather appears as such through speech whose tone is recognized. [Amuka...]
Thus, it is in the masculine gender by virtue of intending to express the meaning of the word. //51//

"Āḥ sarvataḥ," and so forth. "Āḥ" is used in the sense of pain (*pīḍā*); according to Amara, "āstu syāt kopapīḍayoḥ" (the particle *āḥ* may be used in the sense of anger and pain). Here, *pīḍā* means suffering (*duḥkha*).
There are two imperative forms (*loṭ*).
"At the proper time" (prāptakāle); the meaning is that the times for [the moon's] quivering and for drinking have arrived.
By this explanation, there is no room for the objection that it is a description of moonlight out of context. "Pungent-sweet" (kaṣāyamadhurām) means fragrant-sweet.
For it has been stated: "Pungent, bitter, and astringent [tastes] are also proclaimed [to be present] in fragrance. Regarding this:
The intoxication of liquor; or [a substance] having an astringent or sweet taste;
as it has been said: "Hot and pungent, heat produces *pitta*; shade..."

"Moonlight is sweet and cool; it is traditionally held to be astringent-sweet, pungent-bitter, and cold. (208) Thus, it is designated by that name because it performs those functions. In the word *paṅkeruha*, there is no elision [of the case-ending] according to the rule "after a consonant or a vowel ending in 'a'... (209). For indeed, in the case of a lamp, during its burning...
It is established here that, when the restrainer has departed, the engagement of rogues in improper paths is implied. //52//
"Thick," and so forth. "Timira" means darkness itself;
"ghuṇa" refers to a specific type of wood-eating insect. "Of the kāṣṭhas" means of the directions (kāṣṭha) and of woods (dāru).
"With the stars in the form of apertures"—the meaning is "by way of the paths"; the instrumental case is used here in the sense of the instrument (karaṇe tṛtīyā). //53//
"nirmajjad" and so forth: "nirmajjatoḥ" means "of the two who are submerged.
"Krūrā" means difficult to look upon; she whose pupils (tārā) are such is [krūratārā].
"Grathitam" means fixed or stuck. "Ghaṭṭayantī" means causing it to move or extracting it.

*Vyātta* means opened wide; *jarjara* means loosened. This is an adjective containing a reason (*hetugarbhita*): even though darkness exists, it has been destroyed by the flames of fire from his mouth.
This means the manifestation of karma. "The flight of vultures" is a sign of death. Regarding the word *parikrīḍate*:
the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to Pāṇini 1.3.21, which states that the root *krīḍ* takes the middle voice when preceded by *anu*, *sam*, or *pari*. //54//
"Three," and so forth. "Having filled the *kuṇḍas*": the meaning is that they rain for as long as it takes to fill the *kuṇḍas*, which is the measure of the rainfall.
The suffix *ṇamul* is applied by the rule "ūlopaś cāsya anyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 3.4.17).
*Parivṛṇvate* means they envelop or surround. //55//
"Vidhānam" and so forth. "Ānuśravika" means "derived from revelation" (śrauta); the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied because it belongs to the class beginning with "adhyātma.
"Pratiṣkirantī" means "destroying"; the augment *suṭ* is added by the rule "hiṃsāyāṃ prateśca."
"By *ātatāyins*," meaning those intent on killing; according to Amara, "an *ātatāyin* is one intent on killing"; by this, the fact that they are to be slain is stated.
As it has been said: "One should indeed slay an approaching assassin without hesitation. (216) //56//
*Ghṛṇā* means compassion (*kṛpā*), used in the feminine sense; according to the *Vaijayantī*, "ghṛṇā" [occurs] in the meanings of loathing (*jugupsā*) and compassion (*kṛpā*). (217)
"Bhagavan," and so forth. By saying "a woman," he expresses her pitiable state; the ellipsis is "how shall I restrain her? *Abrahmaṇyam* means "one who should not be killed";
Amara states: "The word *abrahmaṇyam* is used when speaking of one who is not to be slain. (218)

"Enough," and so forth. "Enough of being afflicted" means that affliction should not be committed. [The form] *kliśitvā* is derived from the root *kliś* with the suffixes *ktvā* and *niṣṭhā*, where the augment *iṭ* is applied by the rule *kliśaḥ ktvāniṣṭhayoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.50). Due to the rule *mṛḍamṛda-* (Pāṇini 1.2.7), there is an absence of *guṇa* because of the *kit* designation. [The form] *alam* is derived according to the rule *alaṃ khalvoḥ* (Pāṇini 3.4.18) and others.
The suffix *ktvā*;
this rule consists in the slaying of the Rākṣasa;
the son of Dharma is the disciple. //57//

"Let it not be done"; Vardhamāna states that *kṛtam* is used in the sense of warding off or prohibition (*nivāraṇa-niṣedha*). The instrumental case in *uttarottareṇa* is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇe*).
The meaning is that there is no further goal to be accomplished through successive stages.
"Nedīyān" means proximate or near.
Regarding the word "mīmāṃsate" and so forth: "mīmāṃsate" means he investigates or deliberates.

By the rule "mānbadha" (Pāṇini 3.1.6), the suffix *san* is applied to express a desire to know (*jijñāsā*). The scripture follows their very speech; the scripture is nothing other than their utterance.
This is the section on *bhāva* (the state of being).
From here until the verse ending with "our words" (*vacāṃsi naḥ*), it is called the ornament named *upadiṣṭa* (the instructed), because it proceeds in accordance with the scriptures.
As it has been said: "A statement that accords with the meaning of the scripture is declared to be 'taught by that' (tadupadiṣṭaka). (227) //58//
"Weighty," and so forth. The dative case in *adharmāya* is used in the sense of "for the sake of" (*tādarthye*). *Mīlitākṣaiḥ* means "by those who possess forbearance.
[This refers to] those whose lives are momentary.
The sense is: "What is there to be ashamed of? //59//
"Long," and so forth.
"By those exceedingly curious" means by those eager to find fault. "In this" refers to the act of killing a woman.
"Witness" means one who has seen it directly; that is to say, one who has not perished. In this context—

The *Lalla-saṃhitā* states: "The seven sages, Kratu, Pulaha, and the others—of these, three at a time are liberated. Yet in every kalpa, Vasiṣṭha remains in the station of Arundhatī, which is honored by the world. (229)
The word "guru" states the cause for shame. //60//
"Alam," and so forth: "alam" means that the sacrifice (iṣṭvā) should not be performed;
"adavīyān" means not distant.
It is correct [to say] "sthūladūra" and so forth. This [sword], which has the form of a razor's edge; "upatiṣṭhate" means it comes into contact; [from the root] "upa-ā..."

The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used in the phrase "devapūjā" (231) and so forth. As for the sword, its distance [from the result] is due to the fact that, once the fall of the body has occurred by the force of having commenced the sacrifice (*makha*), it subsequently leads to the attainment of heaven. However, as for the sword...

Because it brings about the attainment of heaven immediately, there is no distance [to be traversed]; as it has been said: "There are only two persons in this world who pierce the solar orb: the wandering mendicant absorbed in yoga, and one who is slain facing the enemy in battle. (232) //61//
"Daśaratha," and so forth. "Who is this? means "this is someone [unknown]"; the sense is that he is utterly to be shunned.
Just as a sprout, by means of its own support, might overrun a pavilion and the like, so too will he, by means of my support, overrun the entire lineage.
Thus, "he doubts" means he is in a state of uncertainty; Amara states, "vicikitsā, however, is doubt" (233). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "may that doubt not arise. [That which...]
Because, regarding the subject matter of Dharma, the court of justice—the authoritative scripture—is for you nothing other than your own words;
for the *Kāśikā* (2.3.4) states: "The judge (*stheya*) is the one who decides the points of dispute."
"Rajanī" and so forth. "Apāsyan" means for the sake of removing (*apāsanāya*); the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) is used here in the sense of a causal motive (*hetau*).
"Ayam" means precisely that which is connected to this very moment; the sense is "without delay. "Toyabinduḥ" (a drop of water).

The term *ābhicārikaḥ* refers to a secondary method (*anukalpam*), which is subordinate (*gauṇam*). As Amarasimha states: "The primary method is the first option (*mukhyaḥ syāt prathamaḥ kalpaḥ*), while the secondary method is inferior to that (*anukalpastu tato'dhamaḥ*). (236)
In the same way, the sense is that it is unfailing. //63//

"Diṣṭyā" is an indeclinable used in the sense of joy. (237) Whether victory comes or not, the meaning of the word "tāvat" is that the preparation for battle has occurred by good fortune; when, then, will my youth bear fruit?

Or [it may be understood as] "it will be. Regarding the passage beginning with "purastāt" and so forth: in the compound *dhṛtadhanuṣī*, because the rule for forming compound endings (*samāsāntavidhi*) is not universally obligatory (*anityatva*), the suffix *anaṅ* prescribed by the rule *dhanuṣaśca* does not occur.
"Vāyavya," and so forth. Tāṭakeya is Mārīca; [the suffix] *ḍhak* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.1.120 (*strībhyo ḍhak*).
He is "living dead."

Because she has fled; "cut" means compassion (*karuṇā*) because of the inability to endure the suffering of others; it is a marvel that she possesses the strength of a thousand elephants yet is struck by a fool, as seen through the appearance of blood and so forth.

There is disgust; laughter because she has come to kill [him] and has been killed; terror because of her horrific appearance; anger from remembering a previous injury; and, due to his being a seer (*ṛṣi*), the initial arising of compassion; by these emotions, he was *uttarala*—that is, agitated.

By the mention here of the slaying of Subāhu and others who were *ātatāyins* (aggressors), this is what is called "slaying" (*vadha*), a subordinate element (*upāṅga*) known as a "transition" (*sandhyantara*). As it has been said: "Slaying, however, is an act that threatens life."
It may be [the case] regarding an assailant. //64// (241)
"O child," and so forth. "Dependent on others" (*paravantaḥ*) means being under the control of others;
the meaning is that due to being overwhelmed by wonder and joy, one lacks the power to offer praise. For one who is dependent on others [is unable to act] in what ought to be done by oneself.
It is not desired; rather, it must be spoken of, meaning it must be praised—because the protection afforded by Indra and others is common to all members of your lineage. In this regard:
The meaning is: "What praise can be yours? He states this very point with the words beginning with "na khalu" (not indeed), etc.
*Pratiṣṭhā* means greatness (*māhātmya*). From here until the passage "cāturyamadhyāpitaḥ" (243).
The final limb is named *paribhāvanā*, which consists of the experience of wonder (*adbhutāvedana*).

As it has been said: "Wonder (*paribhāva*) is the experience of marvel" (244). This quality of wonderfulness consists in [the fact that] humans are the subduers of Rākṣasas and the benefactors of the gods.
He states the very foundation [of the teaching] with the words beginning with "direction" (*dig*) and so forth. "Kūlaṅkaṣāḥ" means pervading;
[the suffix] *khac* is applied according to the rule "sarvakūla" (Pāṇini 3.2.42).
"Nirvyāja" means without artifice.

They are heroes by their very nature; the meaning is that while people generally exert their prowess when faced with humiliation, these [people] do not act in such a way. "By whom" refers to you. The particle *api* is used here in the sense of possibility.
"By those who bear... and so forth; the meaning is that because you yourselves have accomplished all that was to be done, he has become merely devoted to women. //65//
"Today," and so forth. Having made the *ādhāna*—that is, the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*)—for the "heroic dharma," which is battle;
[the meaning is] that this is not actually a battle, but merely the resolve for it. This is an expression of Rāma’s extraordinary enthusiasm. //66//

*Vailakṣyam* means shame, specifically that caused by the killing of a woman. He expresses this very point with the words beginning "Pūṣā" and so forth. *Straiṇaḥ* means relating to women (*strī-sambandhī*);
the suffix *nañ* is applied here according to the rule "from *strī* and *pums*" (Pāṇini 5.1.246).
This object, consisting of the nature of pleasure and pain, is the limb called *vidhāna*;
as it has been said: "The *vidhāna* is that which produces pleasure and pain. [Regarding] pleasure...
Suffering arose from failing to carry out the guru's command, and from the shame of having killed a woman. //67//

"Pratyāsanna" and so forth: "by means of strengthening factors" (*balyābhiḥ*) means by causes for strength; the suffix *yat* is applied here according to the rule "godvyaco'saṅkhyā" (Pāṇini 5.1.39). "With indistinct features" (*sammīlitavyañjanāḥ*) means having unclear characteristics.
The meaning is that even the thin darkness became dense due to contact with smoke.
"Tomorrow" (śvaḥ) means on the following day at dawn.
"About to be put on" (sañcīvarayiṣyamāṇāḥ) means about to be worn.

By the rule beginning with *pucchabhāṇḍa* (Pāṇini 3.1.20), the suffix *ṇiṅ* is applied in the sense of wearing (*paridhāna*). [The term refers to] that which has not been washed, that which has been washed by a washerman, and that which was indeed washed on the previous day.

The prohibition [of wearing] "ca" (251) refers to the prohibition of wearing [the garment] in contexts other than the morning bath, or specifically regarding *śrāddha* ceremonies. Those very [garments] are those washed by young boys (*vaṭuka*). "Nidrāṇāḥ" means lying down; [this refers to the rule] "after a root beginning with a conjunct consonant and ending in /ā/" (*saṃyogāder ātaḥ*).
The substitution of *ṇ* for the final consonant of a verbal root ending in *yaṇ* occurs before the suffix *niṣṭhā*. //68//
"Throbbling," and so forth. "Mādyan-mādyat" means "intoxicated, becoming intoxicated";
it is a reduplication used to express the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*). [This was said] by Datta. (253)
"By her own hand" means by the support of her hand; "thick" means dense, due to the accumulation of like particles.
"O beloved," let there not be "lightness of heart" on the part of those whose "sight"—that is, their gaze—is fixed upon you, arising from the abandonment of pride.
Because a *pratibhū*— that is, a guarantor (*lagnaka*)—
stands as an intermediary between the creditor and the debtor; he "anoints" (or manifests) [the truth],
lest there be a secret meeting of proud women with their lovers, since [this occurs] upon the rising of the moon.

The sense is that the lovers, pained by separation, will come together of their own accord; or else, in the context of the lightness of the heart (*hṛdayalaghiman*), *āgūḥ* means a promise (*pratijñā*).
According to Amarasimha, "saṃvidāgūḥ pratijñānam" (a promise or agreement);

by that [means], the sense is "by means of going to meet. He is the guarantor for that sight of the beloved which occurs through her [going to meet him]; that is, one who brings about the sight of such beloveds.
This is the meaning. //69//
"Unmīlantī" and so forth. "Saṃvartikā" refers to the nine petals;
Amara states: "Saṃvartikā means a nine-petaled [lotus]. Saṃvarta means destruction itself, which is their vow (*vrata*);
those whose activity (*vṛtti*) is directed toward that [destruction] are the *saṃvartikāḥ*. By reason of the universe emerging, ...

*Kṣubdhaḥ* means "like one who is agitated," due to the churning of his sides. For this very reason, he "[phenāyata iva] = seems to emit foam"; the suffix *kyaṅ* is used here in the sense of emission according to the rule: *phenācceti vaktavyam* (Vārttika 256).
The sense is that the white mountain peaks appear like foam;
just as, for instance, when lifting a jar or similar object submerged in a well, first—
The meaning is that, in this case as well, it is like the emergence of a bubble. //70//
"Indu," and so forth. That being so, let it not be [the case] even now. By the word *nāsīra*, the vanguard (*agrabhāga*) is indicated.
Because there, the rays (*tviṣ*) cause delight—that is, they make fragrant—therefore, [it occurs] precisely before the rising.
Since his own duty has been accomplished, not only is his arising useless,
but it also reveals his inherent defect.
This is the state; from this very [state] arises world-weariness (nirveda). //71//
He states the significance of the moonrise with the words beginning "with saffron" (*kāśmīreṇa*), etc.
"With saffron" (*kāśmīreṇa*) means with *kuṅkuma*; "smearing" (*dihānam*) means anointing; [as in the phrase] "born in Kashmir, like a flame of fire."
Thus says Amara (257).

This is a statement containing a simile (*upamāgarbhokti*), because of the extreme redness at the time of sunrise. The state of two kings is *dvairājyam*; the compound is formed according to the rule beginning with "taddhitārtha" (Pāṇini 2.1.51). (258)
Because [the word] *brāhmaṇa* and others belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied; thus, it means "rivaling the face of a woman.
*Ambhaḥsirāḥ* refers to the water-carrying channels. *Pratyudyatyaḥ* means "coming forth to meet."
*Kṣībaḥ* means intoxicated. //72//

"Paulomī," and so forth. "By means of [her] passion" (*rajasā*); "in which birth there was kinship" (*svājanyam*)—that is, the state of being a relative—this is a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* compound; by that [passion], they were arrogant, even toward those on the king's side.

Because those on the side of the goddesses are arrogant—that is to say, they are impassioned—they "adorn" (upaskurvate), meaning they decorate [themselves]. The augment *suṭ* is applied according to the rule beginning with "samparyupa" (Pāṇini 6.1.137).
The suffix *śeṣa* is used for the object (*karman*) because of the rule "kṛñaḥ pratiyatne" (Pāṇini 1.4.33), when the object is intended to be expressed as a residual element (*śeṣatvena*).
“Of the boundaries” is the genitive case. “Licking” means swallowing.
“Tying up” means having separated [them] by loosening the knots of darkness.
By those illuminating; by those spreading out—that is, covering; "most internal" means most similar, because of the well-known [Vedic] statement that the sky is blue due to darkness (*tamas*).
That sky, *ojāyate*—meaning it acts like *ojo* (vital energy), i.e., it shines exceedingly intensely; or rather, it shines as something most intimate (*antaratama*), that is, similar to darkness;
the meaning is that by the excess of light, the blueness of the sky became manifest. [This is an example of] the suffix *kyaṅ* after a word denoting the agent.
The suffix *kyaṅ* is also applied [to a word] when preceded by *sa* or *lopa*. (262) //73//

"Naivetyādi": A *gavyūti* is a pair of *krośas*; according to Amara, "a *gavyūti* is feminine and denotes a pair of *krośas*" (263). It has that as its measure (*tat-pramāṇam*); the feminine suffix *ṅīp* is applied by the rule "ṭiḍḍhāṇañ... (264).
*Cāṭukārāḥ* means those who speak kindly, i.e., those who cause [the heart] to blossom.

They seize [it] by the living; that is to say, they seize the darkness while it is still alive. The suffix *ṇamul* is applied according to the rule "samūlākṛtajīveṣu haṇaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.36), and the subsequent use of the verb follows the rule "kaṣādiṣu yathāvidhyanuprayogaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.46).
The verb *gṛhṇāti* is used as an auxiliary (*anuprayoga*). Even now the moon does not rise properly; nevertheless, such is its [power over] darkness.
"Bādha" refers to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) characterized by prowess at the vanguard. //74//
Having observed the abundant moonlight above and the shadow below, he speculates in both ways with the words "What indeed... and so forth.
*Kataka* is a specific type of tree whose seeds clarify water. [Of that...]
"Kṣodaḥ" refers to the powder of its seeds; it is "stained with mud" under the guise of a shadow below, because when the water is clear, the mud sinks to the bottom.
A *kartarī* is an iron implement used as a tool for carving;
it is so called because of its function of carving (*nistakṣaṇa*), that is, making something thin. //75//
"Daletyādi" (and so forth). "Vitatiḥ" means a collection. "Iha tale" means here below.
"Tilataṇḍulitam" means acting like sesame seeds and rice grains because it is variegated by the shadows of leaves; the meaning is that it is similar to that.

According to the rule "In the sense of conduct (ācāra), [the suffix] *kvip* is applied after all nominal stems (*prātipadika*)," some say; thereafter, the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) is applied.
The meaning is that, amidst such radiance, it appears as if empty because it has been swallowed by intoxicated cakora birds. //76//
"Of the three worlds," and so forth. *Luṇṭākyaḥ* means "destructive"; the suffix *ṣākan* is applied according to the rule *jalpabhikṣa* (Pāṇini 4.4.60).
*Mihiraḥ* means the sun. *Abhividhiḥ* means pervasion. [The world] remains [only as a memory], the sense being that it remains in the form of the torment of separation. *Aho* expresses grief.

There is distress because that which pervades the three worlds has become contracted. Directly—that is, by himself—having entered within, he destroys both hunger and darkness; and the moonbeams, with their tips uncut—that is, in their entirety—[are restored].
The *cakora* birds are contemptible (*kutsita*), for they "move about" (*caranti*)—that is, they devour [the moonlight];
the suffix *kap* is applied here according to the rule "after a contemptuous term" (Pāṇini 5.3.89). Thus, even the lunar radiance, which destroys hunger and darkness, is likewise [consumed].
There is also distress regarding the thought that "it perishes. //77//
"Thus," and so forth. "In the eastern direction" (*paurastyāyām*) means in that which is situated in front; [the suffix] *-tyak* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.2.98 (*dakṣiṇāpaścātpurasastyak*).
"Destroying the buds of the lily-fields" (*kumudakedārakalikākapāṭaghnīm*) means possessing the power to destroy the seals of the buds in the fields of white water-lilies.
In the rule "śaktau hastikapāṭayoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.52), the suffix *ṭak* is applied. *Laharīm* means a current or flow.
Likewise, *ullalayati* means she causes to sport or, in other words, impels.

Just as in the case of moonstones (*candrakānta*); "per ball" (*pratiguḍaka*) means per individual instance (*prativyakti*); *guḍaka* is simply *guḍa*; for it is said: "The word *guḍa* [denotes] both a ball and the boiled juice of sugarcane. (273)
Thus says Amara. [The trees] possess clusters of blossoms with droplets opening out on all sides;

they "act like heaps" (*puñjāyante*), meaning they behave as if they were heaps (*puñjavat*). The suffix *kyaṅ* is used here in the sense of an action resembling another (*ācārārthe*). Even though the jewels are separate, they are jagged with water-drops.
The meaning is that they appear as if closely joined together; or, it means that even each individual gem appears like a cluster of gems. //78//
"Taruna" and so forth: that which the moon bears as blue is called its "stain," but that is indeed untrue;
rather, it is the sky itself, characterized by the hollows of the wounds from the merciless teeth-bites of Rāhu.
"This is indeed that" is the figure of speech *apahnava* (concealment); [the suffix] *khaś* is applied by the rule "vidhvaruṣostudaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.35). //79//
"By rays," and so forth: because the sky is filled with rays—that is, with splendors—as if by dust particles split apart by a chisel, and with stars as if by large fragments; therefore [it is so].

Having previously been soiled, it will be somewhat— slightly— polished; moreover, it will fall— that is, it will descend— into the mold, a specific kind of carving tool or machine, of Vidagdha Viśvakarman, who is as if fashioned from the orb of the sun.
The sense is "for the purpose of clearing up the remaining portion.

Alternatively, the suffix *lṛṭ* is used in the sense of possibility (*sambhāvanā*) in the word "bhaviṣyati" (it will be); and "ayam api ca" means "this one too," [the implication being] "since the sky is of such a nature, therefore this one too..."
"Like the sun, he will be on the peak"—that is, he will fall into the machine; the meaning is that he ought to be in the machine.
[This refers to] "the illusory, immovable machines."
According to Amara: "The word *kūṭa* is used in the masculine for heaps of deceit and falsehoods, and in the neuter for an iron mace, a mountain peak, and the pole of a plough.
(277) It is well known that the sun is "carved" [or depicted] [upon the mountain]; [as it is said: "Tvaṣṭṛ..."
"He has carved him like Vivasvat," (278),
meaning: "The hot-rayed one, having mounted the whirling of the wheel,
was carved with effort by Tvaṣṭṛ as it were."
"It shines forth," according to the words of Kālidāsa. //80//
It is not that the moon and the constellations arise [from the earth], but rather that the constellations themselves are the originators of the moon; thus he says:
"Bringing forth abundant darkness," and so forth.

In *tamasvinīṣu*, meaning "on nights of the dark fortnight," the suffix *vini* is applied according to the rule *asmāyā* (Pāṇini 5.2.121). In *jyotsnīṣu*, meaning "on moonlit nights," the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the supplementary rule *aṇprakaraṇe jyotsnādibhya upasaṃkhyānam* (Vārttika on Pāṇini 5.2.103).

"Scattered" means very few. For that reason, we understand [this]; why? Because they have been rolled into balls by the fire called "twilight" within the crucible called "the sky," which is a specific type of earthen vessel.
This is the ornament known as *arthāpatti* (presumption),
because it establishes that the moon is caused by the stars, based on the otherwise inexplicable nature of the waxing and waning of the stars and the simultaneous waxing and waning of the moon.
As it has been said: "The proof of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is the fact that a matter cannot be established otherwise. (282) //81//

Regarding the passage beginning with "yat pīyūṣa" and so forth: by the phrase "tamaḥstoma" and so on, he indicates the great majesty (*mahānubhāvatva*) of the moon; and that [majesty] arises from the destruction of untimely death (*apamṛtyu*) by means of the nectar (*amṛta*). Death (*mṛtyu*) here is the incapacity to perceive forms.

And "premature death" (apamṛtyutvam) is so called because it is destructible by medical treatment and other means; when such a guest has arrived— having come forward (puraḥ), that is, having appeared before one after the setting of the sun (sūryoḍhe)—
[the fires] turn away (parāñci), meaning they are turned back (parāṅmukhāni).
And [the phrase] "petals turned inward" means:
the Lord of Sacrificers (yajvanām patiḥ) is the Moon; having himself arrived as an evening guest, he [transferred] his own sin to the lotuses that had turned their faces away from him.
Having given that which does not produce similarity with a woman's face,
he subsequently receives from her side the merit that does produce similarity with a woman's face; this is like the moon at evening.
This statement is made because of the closing of the lotuses due to their heat.
By this, there is a transgression of the injunction: "One should not turn away a guest who has arrived with the sun for the sake of lodging. [For] he whose guest...
"Returning home with shattered hopes, he departs having given his own misdeeds to him [the host] and taken away his merit. (284) Thus, the resulting transgression is shown. //82//

"Smerā" and so forth: "smerāḥ" means blossomed. By using the feminine gender in the word "diśaḥ" (the quarters), a lack of discrimination is expressed; for women are indeed devoid of discrimination. Regarding "kutsitā mudasya," when the suffix *a* is added in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), it means "possessing contemptible joy. (285) And [it may also mean] "having contemptible joy."
It throbs. "Udarambharayaḥ" means those who nourish their bellies;
the word *udarambhari* is established by the inclusion of the particle *ca* in the rule "phalegrahirātmambhariśca" (Pāṇini 3.2.26). [The light] is of the nature of moonlight.
*Karambha* refers to barley meal mixed with curd; as Amara states: "Karambhas are curd-mixed barley-meals.
By this, his state of wretchedness is indicated.
*dūṣikā* is eye-secretion;
the word *iti* indicates a reason (*hetu*): because [he is] merely designated by the name "Moon" (*sudhāṃśu*) in this [context].
The passion for the directions and so forth has been bound [to him]; what kind of passion is this?
It means it is born from a vision of that which is not the ultimate reality. "Hā" expresses grief. //83//
This elaborate description of the moon, which indicates a swift desire to depart,
is caused by his great fortitude that manifests his *dhīrodātta* (noble and self-controlled) character,
[and serves to conceal] the sin of killing a woman.
This indicates embarrassment; for this very reason, the sage says—(with a joyful smile)—"How so? and so forth.
[The phrase] "of the sage's joyful smile" [is used].
This is because of the connection between Rāma’s victory and his embarrassment. "In the embrace" means in battle.
"Having returned from victory" means having arrived after attaining victory; this is a compound with an ablative case (*pañcamī-samāsa*) used with the elision of the suffix *lyap*. (289)

*hṛṇīyamānaḥ* means *lajjamānaḥ* (feeling ashamed). According to the rule *hṛṇīṅ toṣe lajjāyāṃ ca* (the root *hṛṇīṅ* is used in the senses of satisfaction and shame), and *kaṇḍvādibhyo yak* (the suffix *yak* is added after roots such as *kaṇḍū*), the sense is that one who is ashamed walks slowly.
Regarding the phrase *asmākam* and so forth: "this which... [refers to him].
The meaning is that the event is equal to the onset of night (*pradoṣaśrī*); for that which is being restated (*anuvādya*) must be something comparable.
He states this very point with the words beginning "of the night-stalkers" (*niśācarāṇām*), etc.; [it occurs] at night.

Of the *rākṣasa*s wandering about and of the *tamas* [demons]; Rāmacandra, the son of Daśaratha, and the moon that delights the mind; possessing the night-lotuses which are the eyes of the sages—the suffix *-mat* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvartha*).
The suffix *ḍmatup* is applied according to the rule beginning with "kumuda-naḍa-vetasa" (Pāṇini 4.2.87). *Ajani* means "born," according to the rule "dīpa-jana" (Pāṇini 3.1.65).
By [the rule] beginning with "ityādinā," the affix *ciṇ* is applied to the agent (*kartari*). //84//
"Intoxicates," and so forth. Because he is equal toward his own people and others alike,
and because even Indra’s vessel of nectar satisfies all the immortals, he therefore acts rightly due to his excellent character (*sauśīlya*).
This is the meaning. //85//
"Salute [me]," he says; the non-mention of his own name and lineage is due to the embarrassment caused by the killing of a woman. "Exalted," and so forth.

"Intending the agent" (*kartṛbhiprāyāṇi*) means those [actions] whose fruits belong to the performer; "prescriptions" (*vidhīn*) refers to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and other such rites, according to the etymological derivation that they are so called because they are "enjoined" (*vidhīyante*). When the *rakṣas* have been slain by you...
The meaning is: "May the fruits of performance accrue only to the sacrificers. In the phrase "paripālyāmahai," the *loṭ* (imperative) mood is used in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*). (294)
"Vīra" contains the seed-syllable (hetu). //86//
"Yatsatyam" means "truthfully";
it signifies that which is like that, similar to that word. "Amunā" implies "by this," meaning by something equal to this.
"By *vyatikara* means by a crush or by a calamity; for there is the lexical definition: 'Even in the case of a calamity, there is a *vyatikara*. (295)

*Vaitānika* means relating to a sacrifice (*kratu*); *kampita* means shaken. The implication is "out of fear. The meaning is: "I am afraid because of the possibility of an affliction by demons in his sacrifice, just as in mine.
The reason for the fear is that he is a dear friend, for it has been said: "The hearts of kinsmen are suspicious of misfortune" (296).
From this point until the conclusion of the act, because it indicates the primary subject matter such as Sītā’s marriage and so forth, it is the dramatic element named *karaṇa*.
As it has been said: "The instrument is the undertaking of what is at hand" (297).
"O child," and so forth. Videha is a specific region. From this point until the end of the passage, "and a human being not born from a womb" (298).
The ornament called *manoratha* (the expression of desire) is the communication of a longing for Sītā under the pretext of describing her native city;
as it has been said: "But *manoratha* is the communication of what one intends to say by means of a pretext. (299)
Thus [ends the section on] the sage’s laughter regarding the subject of stringing the bow of Lord Śiva, which had been the bride-price for Sītā’s marriage.
Because of his complete understanding of Rāma’s intention.
Regarding the passage beginning with "asau" (he): *dyumaṇeḥ* means from the sun (*sūrya*). [This is governed by] Pāṇini 1.4.29:
*ākhyātopayoge* ("In the case of instruction, the source is called *apādāna*").
Thus [is established] its status as the ablative (*apādāna*). "By means of the mouth" (*mukhena*) means "by way of.
"He who studied the *Brahmasaṃhitā*," that is, the *Upaniṣad*, "he is the king"—this is the construction. The phrase "in that" (*tasyām*) connects with what precedes. //87//
There is doubt regarding the violation of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the loss of the vow (*vrata*),
because, by virtue of having renounced weapons and being initiated, one is averse to violence.

"Pratiṣṭhāmahe" means "we shall set out this very day"; the present tense (*laṭ*) is used here because of the proximity to the present time. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is employed according to the rule beginning with "samava-pra. (Pāṇini 1.3.22).

Because Rāma’s angry smile reveals his own intention and because of his affection, he expresses that [the other] is undesired. He provides the rule for *prahasana*: *prahasana* is a dramatic form (*rūpaka*) in which laughter is predominant.

"Sūtrayati" means "he makes a sūtra"; the causative suffix (ṇic) is applied according to the rule "The addition 'tat karoti' [is made] for the sake of forms such as 'sūtrayati'" (Pāṇini 3.1.26 vārttika). It thus means "he composes a sūtra of the *Prahasana*. In the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*), the word "sūtra" [is used].

Because it possesses gender and number, it denotes a specific sentence that is a constituent part of the *prahasana* (farce) and has the nature of a substance (*dravya*); thus, the genitive case in "of the *prahasana*" is based on the relationship between the part and the whole. However, when the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is applied...

Since the verbal root *sū* denotes the meaning of "producing" (*karoti*), which constitutes the sense of the suffix, it is born; thus, because there is no connection with "laughter" (*prahasana*), the genitive case is precluded. When an object is required, "laughter" itself serves as that object.
In an applied sentence (*prayogavākya*), only the accusative case occurs. Haradatta has stated this very point under the rule *hetumati ca* (Pāṇini 3.1.26).
Regarding the word *aṅka*: its status as a "mark" (*aṅkatva*) arises from the fact that it is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) through the deeds of Rāma.
